articles.title: ESMA Issues New Guidance to Prevent Greenwashing in Impact, Climate Claims
articles.summary:
The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) has issued new guidance to improve transparency around sustainability claims in European financial markets. The two thematic notes address positive impact investing and […]
The post ESMA Issues New Guidance to Prevent Greenwashing in Impact, Climate Claims appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
ESMA Issues New Guidance to Prevent Greenwashing in Impact, Climate Claims
- Greenwashing prevention: ESMA publishes two new thematic notes targeting sustainability claims across investment funds, bonds and benchmarks.
- Greater transparency: Financial institutions must clearly explain their impact objectives, transition strategies, measurement methods and underlying assumptions.
- Regulatory alignment: The guidance reinforces existing disclosure expectations without introducing new rules, as the EU reviews its Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR).
The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) has issued new guidance to improve transparency around sustainability claims in European financial markets. The two thematic notes address positive impact investing and climate transition claims, areas facing growing scrutiny over greenwashing risks.
The publications focus on how asset managers, bond issuers and benchmark providers communicate environmental and social ambitions to investors. ESMA wants market participants to substantiate their claims with clear explanations of objectives, implementation strategies and measurable outcomes.
The guidance arrives as European policymakers review the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR), a central component of the EU’s sustainable finance framework.
Impact Investing Faces Greater Transparency Expectations
ESMA’s first thematic note examines how investment funds and bonds communicate claims about generating positive environmental or social impact.
The regulator found that market participants interpret positive impact differently, with considerable variation in the ambition behind their claims.
Some investment products may seek measurable environmental improvements, while others pursue broader sustainability objectives. These distinctions can become difficult for investors to assess when marketing materials lack sufficient detail.
ESMA encourages financial institutions to explain three fundamental elements: the positive difference they intend to make, the mechanisms supporting that impact and the methods used to measure results.
This approach aims to help investors distinguish between products that finance sustainable activities and those seeking to demonstrate additional positive outcomes.
For asset managers, the guidance places greater importance on connecting investment strategies with credible impact measurement.
It also raises expectations around how sustainability objectives are presented in fund documentation, promotional materials and investor communications.
Climate Transition Claims Require Evidence and Accountability
The second thematic note focuses on climate transition claims across investment funds, bonds and financial benchmarks.
Unlike claims about historical performance, transition commitments frequently depend on future actions and uncertain outcomes.
Companies and investment products may announce decarbonisation ambitions without fully explaining the assumptions, dependencies or implementation challenges involved.
ESMA identifies these uncertainties as important considerations for investors evaluating transition-related products.
The regulator encourages market participants to communicate their transition ambitions clearly and explain how they intend to achieve them.
Disclosures should also describe how progress will be assessed and reported, including relevant data limitations and external dependencies.
For investors, this creates a clearer basis for evaluating whether transition strategies are supported by credible implementation plans.
The guidance is particularly relevant to financial products exposed to companies undertaking complex decarbonisation programmes.
Such strategies may depend on technological development, regulatory changes, capital expenditure and wider economic conditions.
Transparent communication about these dependencies can help investors assess execution risks rather than relying solely on long-term climate commitments.
RELATED ARTICLE: ESMA Introduces Measures to Enhance Corporate Sustainability Reporting
Guidance Reinforces Existing Regulatory Standards
ESMA’s thematic notes provide practical examples of effective and ineffective sustainability communications based on observed market practices.
They include recommended approaches and practices to avoid when making sustainability claims outside formal regulatory disclosures.
The central principle remains that financial communications must be clear, fair and not misleading.
Importantly, the publications do not introduce additional regulatory obligations or prescribe specific sustainability ambitions.
ESMA also clarifies that the notes should not be interpreted as determining requirements under the ongoing SFDR review.
Instead, they explain how existing communication standards apply to sustainability-related claims.
The latest publications build on earlier thematic notes addressing ESG credentials and ESG investment strategies.
Together, the series seeks to improve consistency across sustainability communications while reducing opportunities for misleading representations.
Implications for Financial Institutions and Global Investors
For financial executives, the guidance increases the practical importance of governance over sustainability marketing and investor disclosures.
Asset managers and product providers may need to review how impact objectives, transition pathways and performance indicators are communicated across investment materials.
Clearer explanations of measurement methodologies and assumptions can also support stronger internal oversight of sustainability commitments.
For institutional investors, more consistent claims could improve product comparisons and strengthen due diligence.
The implications extend beyond Europe. International asset managers distributing financial products within EU markets must consider European expectations when communicating sustainability objectives.
As regulators worldwide examine greenwashing risks, ESMA’s approach places greater emphasis on evidence, transparency and accountability.
The broader challenge for sustainable finance remains unchanged: ensuring that environmental and social claims accurately reflect investment strategies and achievable outcomes.
For global capital markets, credible sustainability communications are increasingly central to investor confidence, risk assessment and the integrity of climate-related investment products.

articles.title: Verra Issues First Rice Carbon Credits for 210,000 Tonnes of Emissions Cuts
articles.summary:
Verra has approved the first carbon credits under its Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) methodology for improved rice production systems. The approval brings agricultural methane reductions into the voluntary carbon market […]
The post Verra Issues First Rice Carbon Credits for 210,000 Tonnes of Emissions Cuts appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Verra Issues First Rice Carbon Credits for 210,000 Tonnes of Emissions Cuts
- 210,000 tonnes of emissions avoided: Verra approves the first carbon credits under its updated rice production methodology, supporting methane reductions in India.
- Farmers benefit from carbon revenues: The project combines improved irrigation practices with technical support and revenue sharing for participating farmers.
- Carbon market expansion: Another 13 projects across Asia, Africa, and South America are progressing under the methodology, creating opportunities to finance agricultural methane reductions.
Verra has approved the first carbon credits under its Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) methodology for improved rice production systems. The approval brings agricultural methane reductions into the voluntary carbon market through a project in southern India.
The Core Carbon Sustainable Rice Productions 01 project, registered as Verra Project 3243, has avoided more than 210,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e).
Located in Telangana, a major rice-producing state, the project reduces methane emissions by changing how farmers irrigate and manage their fields.
The approval establishes an initial issuance under VM0051, Verra’s methodology for improved rice production systems. It also provides a practical example of how carbon finance can support lower-emission agricultural practices.
Reducing Methane Through Improved Rice Cultivation
Flooded rice paddies are among the world’s largest agricultural sources of methane, a greenhouse gas with substantially greater short-term warming potential than carbon dioxide.
Traditional rice cultivation often keeps fields continuously submerged. These oxygen-depleted conditions encourage microorganisms that generate methane as organic matter decomposes.
The Indian project addresses this problem through alternate wetting and drying (AWD), an irrigation technique that periodically allows fields to dry before reintroducing water.
This approach increases oxygen availability in the soil, limiting methane-producing microbial activity while maintaining rice cultivation.
Core CarbonX Solutions, the project’s developer, provides participating farmers with field water tubes, technical training, and implementation support.
The equipment helps farmers monitor water levels and determine when irrigation is necessary.
Importantly, the project also shares revenue generated from carbon credit sales with participating farmers.
This arrangement creates a financial incentive for adopting lower-emission agricultural practices. It also connects smallholder participation with the growing market for verified emissions reductions.
Verra Methodology Strengthens Carbon Accounting
The credits were issued under VM0051, Improved Management in Rice Production Systems, which incorporates updated scientific principles for quantifying agricultural greenhouse gas reductions.
The methodology provides a framework for measuring emissions reductions associated with changes in rice cultivation practices.
For carbon credit buyers, the methodology’s measurement requirements are central to assessing the environmental integrity of the resulting credits.
Agricultural emissions are particularly challenging to quantify because soil conditions, water availability, climate, and farming practices vary significantly across locations.
Robust accounting therefore remains essential to determining whether reported reductions reflect measurable changes in emissions.
Beyond improved irrigation, VM0051 also accommodates other approaches to reducing methane.
These include cultivating improved rice varieties and introducing methanotrophic bacteria, which consume methane and can reduce its release into the atmosphere.
The broader scope allows project developers to explore different mitigation strategies while operating within a common carbon accounting framework.
RELATED ARTICLE: Verra Approves First Digitally Verified Carbon Credits
Carbon Finance Expands Across Agricultural Markets
Verra’s registry currently lists 13 additional projects using VM0051 that are either under development or undergoing validation.
These projects span India, Brazil, Vietnam, the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Myanmar, and Madagascar.
Their geographic distribution reflects growing interest in agricultural methane mitigation across major rice-producing markets.
For project developers, the methodology offers a route to generate carbon revenues from farming practices that can otherwise face adoption barriers.
For investors and corporate carbon credit buyers, rice methane projects offer another potential source of verified emissions reductions.
However, credit quality will depend on project-level monitoring, credible baselines, additionality, and the durability of changes in farming practices.
The revenue-sharing model also raises important governance considerations. Transparent benefit distribution and continued farmer participation will influence the credibility and long-term performance of these projects.
Implications for Corporate Climate Strategies
Methane reduction has become an increasingly important component of global climate policy because cutting emissions can deliver relatively rapid climate benefits.
Agriculture remains a difficult sector to decarbonize, particularly in regions where rice production supports food security and rural livelihoods.
Verra’s first issuance under VM0051 demonstrates how carbon market mechanisms can help finance changes in agricultural production without requiring farmers to abandon established crops.
For corporate buyers, the development expands the range of agricultural mitigation opportunities available within the voluntary carbon market.
For policymakers and investors, the larger question is whether these projects can scale while maintaining credible emissions accounting and equitable financial benefits.
With 13 additional projects progressing across multiple countries, the methodology could support wider deployment of methane-reduction practices in global rice production.
Its long-term significance will depend on verified climate outcomes, farmer participation, and sustained demand for high-integrity agricultural carbon credits.

articles.title: Science Based Targets Network Launches Nature 2.0 to Strengthen Corporate Biodiversity Action
articles.summary:
SBTN Introduces Updated Framework for Corporate Nature Targets The Science Based Targets Network (SBTN) has launched Science-Based Targets for Nature 2.0, introducing updated methodologies to help companies address biodiversity loss […]
The post Science Based Targets Network Launches Nature 2.0 to Strengthen Corporate Biodiversity Action appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Science Based Targets Network Launches Nature 2.0 to Strengthen Corporate Biodiversity Action
- Expanded corporate guidance: Science-Based Targets for Nature 2.0 introduces more flexible target-setting pathways, stronger freshwater and land methodologies, and practical implementation tools.
- Growing corporate adoption: More than 300 companies across 40 countries are engaging with SBTN methods, with over 60 validated targets across 18 companies.
- Investor expectations: 93% of investors surveyed in TNFD’s 2026 Status Report want corporate nature targets grounded in science.
SBTN Introduces Updated Framework for Corporate Nature Targets
The Science Based Targets Network (SBTN) has launched Science-Based Targets for Nature 2.0, introducing updated methodologies to help companies address biodiversity loss and nature-related business risks.
Released ahead of the UN Biodiversity Conference (CBD COP17), the framework provides clearer pathways for assessing environmental impacts, setting measurable targets and implementing nature-positive strategies.
The update addresses persistent challenges in corporate biodiversity management, including incomplete environmental data, limited supply chain traceability and complex global sourcing networks.
For businesses facing growing exposure to ecosystem degradation, these challenges carry financial consequences. Nature-related dependencies increasingly influence supply security, operational resilience and market access.
“Nature loss is accelerating, and companies cannot afford to wait for perfect data, perfect visibility, or perfect conditions before they act. Science-Based Targets for Nature 2.0 gives companies a pragmatic way to move now — focusing effort where it matters most, while maintaining the scientific rigor and accountability needed for action to be credible.” Erin Billman, CEO, Science Based Targets Network
Expanded Methodologies Address Freshwater, Land and Supply Chain Risks
Science-Based Targets for Nature 2.0 introduces additional pathways that accommodate different levels of corporate readiness, data availability and supply chain visibility.
Companies can now pursue focused target scopes, supplier engagement targets and phased validation processes.
Freshwater methodologies have expanded to strengthen groundwater assessments and incorporate pesticide-related water quality impacts.
Updated land methodologies provide additional approaches for regeneration and restoration. They also extend applicability to mining, infrastructure, construction and extractive industries.
New implementation resources under Step 4: Act support companies transitioning from target-setting to operational planning.
Despite greater flexibility, SBTN maintains independent validation, transparent disclosure and location-specific environmental assessments as central requirements.
“The goal is not simply to make it easier for companies to set more targets. It is to make rigorous science more usable in the decisions companies are actually making — where to focus, what level of action is needed and how to build credible progress over time.” Dr Varsha Vijay, Technical Director, Science Based Targets Network
Investor Demand Drives Greater Accountability
Investor expectations are increasing pressure on companies to demonstrate measurable biodiversity outcomes.
According to the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) 2026 Status Report, 93% of surveyed investors want corporate nature targets to be science-based.
This demand reflects growing recognition that biodiversity degradation can affect asset valuations, financing decisions and long-term business performance.
Corporate participation in SBTN methodologies is also expanding.
More than 300 companies across 40 countries are engaging with the network’s methods. Another 45 companies have publicly committed their intention to establish science-based nature targets.
More than 60 land and freshwater targets have received validation across 18 companies.
SBTN’s Step Up for Nature: The Business Case for Science-Based Targets report identifies additional operational benefits.
Participating companies report greater confidence in allocating resources, prioritizing environmental interventions and engaging suppliers.
RELATED ARTICLE: Science Based Targets Network Releases Updated Guidance for Science-Based Targets on Nature
Alignment With TNFD and Nature Positive Initiative
The framework arrives alongside updates from TNFD and the Nature Positive Initiative (NPI), strengthening coordination across corporate biodiversity assessment and reporting systems.
TNFD provides guidance for identifying and disclosing nature-related dependencies, impacts, risks and opportunities.
SBTN translates relevant assessments into science-based targets and implementation strategies.
The organizations have strengthened methodological alignment, allowing companies to reuse environmental data and analysis across reporting and target-setting activities.
Meanwhile, NPI’s State of Nature Indicators and Metrics initiative establishes a common foundation for measuring ecosystem conditions.
Together, these developments aim to reduce reporting duplication while improving consistency between environmental assessments, corporate disclosures and operational decisions.
Implications for Corporate Strategy and Global Biodiversity Goals
For executives and investors, Nature 2.0 offers a more structured approach to integrating biodiversity considerations into enterprise risk management and capital allocation.
Its introduction ahead of CBD COP17 places corporate accountability within broader international efforts to implement global biodiversity commitments.
SBTN expects future methodological development to concentrate on targeted refinements and supporting tools, apart from a forthcoming ocean-focused update.
That stability could help companies develop longer-term implementation strategies without repeatedly adjusting to major methodological changes.
As governments assess progress against international biodiversity objectives, credible corporate targets will become increasingly important in connecting private-sector investment with measurable environmental outcomes.

articles.title: EBA Releases Reporting Framework 4.4 with Updated Pillar 3 ESG Disclosures
articles.summary:
EBA Advances Banking Reporting and ESG Disclosure Requirements The European Banking Authority (EBA) has released the final technical package for version 4.4 of its reporting and disclosure framework. The update […]
The post EBA Releases Reporting Framework 4.4 with Updated Pillar 3 ESG Disclosures appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
EBA Releases Reporting Framework 4.4 with Updated Pillar 3 ESG Disclosures
- ESG Risk Transparency: The EBA’s reporting framework 4.4 introduces updated Pillar 3 disclosures covering ESG risks, equity exposures and shadow banking activities.
- Regulatory Efficiency: New IFRS 18-aligned reporting templates aim to reduce compliance costs and improve consistency across European banking institutions.
- Further Simplification Ahead: A second implementation phase, expected in early 2027, will introduce additional supervisory reporting simplifications following the EBA’s 2026 consultation.
EBA Advances Banking Reporting and ESG Disclosure Requirements
The European Banking Authority (EBA) has released the final technical package for version 4.4 of its reporting and disclosure framework. The update introduces revised Pillar 3 ESG disclosures, IFRS 18-aligned financial reporting templates and technical amendments across several regulatory areas.
The package forms the first phase of a broader implementation programme designed to improve reporting consistency while reducing compliance costs for European banks.
It also provides the technical infrastructure needed to implement updated disclosure requirements covering environmental, social and governance risks, equity exposures and shadow banking activities.
For financial institutions, the changes affect how regulatory information is structured, validated and submitted. They also support greater comparability of financial and sustainability-related risk information across the European banking sector.
Updated Pillar 3 ESG Disclosures Strengthen Risk Transparency
A central component of release 4.4 concerns amendments to Pillar 3 disclosure requirements.
The framework incorporates updated reporting specifications for ESG risks, equity exposures and shadow banking activities. These reflect the EBA’s final draft amendments to the Pillar 3 Implementing Technical Standards (ITS).
Selected disclosure templates relating to the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) are also included.
Pillar 3 disclosures provide market participants with information about banks’ risk exposures, capital adequacy and risk management practices.
The revised technical framework supports more consistent disclosure of ESG-related financial risks. This is particularly relevant as European supervisors continue integrating climate and environmental considerations into banking oversight.
For investors, standardized disclosures can improve comparisons between institutions and strengthen assessments of financial resilience.
However, the technical package primarily implements existing and amended reporting requirements rather than introducing a separate set of ESG obligations.
IFRS 18 Reporting Changes Target Greater Financial Consistency
The EBA has also introduced a new Financial Reporting (FINREP) module aligned with International Financial Reporting Standard 18.
IFRS 18 introduces changes to the presentation and disclosure of financial information, including income and expenses.
The updated FINREP templates will operate alongside the EBA’s previously published Opinion on implementing IFRS 18 in supervisory financial reporting.
The objective is to facilitate earlier IFRS 18-compliant reporting while maintaining consistency between financial statements and supervisory submissions.
The package also includes European Central Bank data collection requirements for FINREP data points submitted by less significant institutions.
However, the EBA clarified that it will not collect this information directly.
These changes will require affected institutions to assess their reporting systems, data classifications and internal controls against the revised technical specifications.
RELATED ARTICLE: EBA Opens Consultation on ESG Risk Management Guidelines for Financial Institutions
Technical Amendments Extend Beyond ESG Reporting
Release 4.4 also addresses technical inconsistencies across several supervisory and resolution reporting areas.
The package includes corrections to Data Point Models (DPM) and XBRL taxonomies covering resolution planning, Minimum Requirement for Own Funds and Eligible Liabilities (MREL) decisions and Pillar 3 disclosures.
These amendments address issues previously identified in the EBA’s published list of known DPM problems.
Additional corrections apply to third-country branch liquidity reporting, particularly template E 09.02.
The release also incorporates Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) eligibility templates and revised reporting specifications supporting the authority’s 2027 risk assessment data collection exercise.
Together, these updates aim to reduce technical inconsistencies that can complicate regulatory submissions and increase operational costs.
Further Reporting Simplification Expected in 2027
The EBA plans to deliver the second phase of framework 4.4 in early 2027.
That phase will implement the supervisory reporting simplification package consulted on between April and July 2026.
The proposals are currently being finalized and are expected to deliver additional reductions in reporting complexity.
For banking executives, the immediate priority is preparing reporting infrastructure for the revised technical requirements while anticipating further changes.
Compliance teams will need to coordinate financial reporting, ESG risk disclosures and regulatory data management to maintain consistency across submissions.
The broader significance extends beyond operational efficiency. As European banking supervision increasingly incorporates sustainability-related financial risks, reliable and comparable disclosures remain central to market transparency.
The EBA’s phased approach seeks to balance those transparency requirements with efforts to reduce regulatory burdens, a continuing priority for European banks and policymakers.

articles.title: Impact Carbon Appoints Christopher Morgan Zink CEO to Drive Carbon Market Growth
articles.summary:
Impact Carbon has appointed Christopher Morgan Zink as Chief Executive Officer, effective September 30, strengthening its leadership as international carbon markets move towards stricter integrity standards and expanding compliance demand. […]
The post Impact Carbon Appoints Christopher Morgan Zink CEO to Drive Carbon Market Growth appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Impact Carbon Appoints Christopher Morgan Zink CEO to Drive Carbon Market Growth
- Leadership Transition: Christopher Morgan Zink takes over as CEO, bringing nearly two decades of experience in international carbon finance and compliance markets.
- Climate and Development Impact: Impact Carbon’s programmes reach more than 1.2 million households with efficient cooking solutions and 24 million students with safe drinking water.
- Carbon Market Expansion: The company is positioning for growth as demand shifts towards high-integrity carbon credits, Article 6 mechanisms and compliance markets.
Impact Carbon has appointed Christopher Morgan Zink as Chief Executive Officer, effective September 30, strengthening its leadership as international carbon markets move towards stricter integrity standards and expanding compliance demand.
Zink joins from Conservation International, where he served as Vice President and led the organisation’s global carbon finance activities. His appointment comes as governments and corporate buyers increasingly seek verified emissions reductions with measurable development benefits.
The leadership transition places an experienced carbon finance executive at the helm of a company operating across Uganda, Nigeria and Kenya.
Leadership Change Positions Impact Carbon for Expansion
Zink brings nearly two decades of experience spanning conservation finance, government policy and commercial carbon markets.
Before joining Conservation International, he spent 15 years working in climate and carbon finance with the Swedish government and Dutch energy trading company Eneco.
His experience covers both public and private carbon financing mechanisms, providing expertise as international markets adapt to new regulatory frameworks.
Impact Carbon’s founders, Evan Haigler and Tim Neville, will remain closely involved in the business. Zink will assume responsibility for day-to-day operations and strategic execution.
Announcing his appointment, Zink said:
“I just started as CEO of Impact Carbon. Impact Carbon is one of the longest-running carbon project developers in the market. Nearly twenty years of taking energy-efficient cooking and safe drinking water to scale, now across Uganda, Nigeria and Kenya, through every phase of the carbon market. The scale is real: well over a million households cooking on efficient stoves, and 24 million students with safe water at school. I’m still wrapping my head around these numbers.”
Carbon Finance Supports Millions Across Africa
Impact Carbon has spent nearly two decades developing carbon programmes that combine emissions reductions with measurable social benefits.
Its energy-efficient cooking initiatives have reached more than 1.2 million households, primarily in Uganda and Nigeria.
These programmes use carbon finance to support access to improved cooking technologies, potentially reducing fuel consumption and associated emissions.
The company also develops and manages carbon programmes supporting Impact Water, a major provider of school-based safe drinking water.
Impact Water currently serves more than 24 million students across 60,000 schools in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
By supporting safe drinking water access, these programmes can reduce reliance on boiling water, which often requires biomass fuels.
The approach connects carbon finance with broader development priorities, including public health, education and access to cleaner energy.
Article 6 and Compliance Markets Shape Growth Strategy
Impact Carbon has historically structured its projects with compliance markets in mind, using voluntary carbon markets to support programme development.
Its experience spans the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), South Korea’s Emissions Trading System (ETS), and emerging opportunities under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.
The company is also targeting demand associated with the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA).
RELATED ARTICLE: Climate Impact Partners Certifies Lob’s Carbon Neutral Offering
Article 6 enables international cooperation on emissions reductions, including transfers of mitigation outcomes between countries under agreed accounting requirements.
For project developers, these mechanisms create potential access to new buyers while increasing expectations around verification, authorisation and environmental integrity.
Zink described the company’s growth ambitions: “The company is in a growth phase, and the market is moving in the direction I have long believed it should: towards higher-quality units, Article 6 and compliance demand. I believe in the long-term fundamentals of carbon finance as a way to pay for things that work for climate and people, in the places that need them most. That is what Impact Carbon does.”
African Carbon Markets Enter a New Phase
Zink’s initial engagements include visits to Impact Carbon’s operations and partners in Kenya and Uganda.
He is also scheduled to speak at the Carbon Markets Africa Summit in Kigali before travelling to Nigeria.
His appointment comes amid growing scrutiny of carbon credit quality, particularly around additionality, emissions accounting and the durability of project benefits.
For investors and corporate buyers, Impact Carbon’s strategy reflects the increasing importance of connecting verified climate outcomes with established delivery systems.
Its expansion will depend on maintaining programme integrity while navigating evolving compliance requirements and buyer expectations.
Across Africa, the broader challenge remains translating carbon market demand into reliable financing for climate and development projects.
Impact Carbon’s leadership transition places that challenge at the centre of its next phase of growth.

articles.title: Africa Nature Impact Fund Targets $100 Million for Carbon, Biodiversity Projects
articles.summary:
Finance Earth, FSD Africa and FSD Africa Investments (FSDAi) have launched a $100 million financing platform to accelerate investment in African nature-based carbon and biodiversity projects. Announced at the Carbon […]
The post Africa Nature Impact Fund Targets $100 Million for Carbon, Biodiversity Projects appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Africa Nature Impact Fund Targets $100 Million for Carbon, Biodiversity Projects
- $100 million investment target: Africa Nature Impact Fund aims to finance early stage nature and carbon projects, with a $20 million first close planned for 2027.
- Climate and biodiversity impact: The fund targets 4.5 million hectares of protected or restored land, more than 100 million tonnes of CO₂e avoided or sequestered, and over 60 species protected.
- Community investment: The platform aims to generate $450 million for local communities while strengthening African ownership of nature-based assets.
Finance Earth, FSD Africa and FSD Africa Investments (FSDAi) have launched a $100 million financing platform to accelerate investment in African nature-based carbon and biodiversity projects.
Announced at the Carbon Markets Africa Summit in Kigali, the Africa Nature Impact Fund aims to address persistent financing gaps affecting early-stage conservation and restoration initiatives.
The platform is targeting a $20 million first close in 2027, supported by a proposed $6.6 million cornerstone commitment from FSDAi.
More than 62% of Africa’s GDP depends on natural capital. Yet investment in biodiversity protection and nature-based carbon projects remains insufficient, limiting opportunities to develop commercially viable conservation initiatives.
Africa Nature seeks to bridge this gap through patient capital, technical support and financing structures that prioritise community participation.
Financing Africa’s Natural Capital
The fund targets the protection or regeneration of 4.5 million hectares of land across Africa.
Its portfolio aims to avoid or sequester more than 100 million tonnes of CO₂e over project lifetimes. It also seeks to protect over 60 animal and plant species.
Beyond environmental outcomes, Africa Nature aims to improve livelihoods for 1.4 million people, with women accounting for half of the beneficiaries.
The financing model builds on FSD Africa’s Carbon Accelerator Programme for the Environment (CAPE), delivered in partnership with Finance Earth.
CAPE has assessed more than 300 projects, developing a pipeline representing over 3.4 billion tonnes of potential CO₂e impact across 76.5 million hectares.
This pipeline provides a foundation for identifying projects capable of attracting institutional investment.
Africa Nature will offer financing across multiple development stages, including project preparation, commercial piloting and implementation.
The approach aims to help projects transition from pre-revenue development into operations supported by sustainable, contracted income.
Community Revenue and African Ownership
Community benefit-sharing forms a central component of the fund’s investment strategy.
Africa Nature will finance projects with meaningful arrangements that allocate a substantial proportion of gross carbon revenue to host communities.
The platform targets approximately $450 million in community benefits over project lifetimes.
It also intends to strengthen African financial institutions’ capacity to finance and manage nature-based assets.
Working alongside FSD Africa and regional partners, the fund will support carbon market readiness among local banks and investors.
This approach seeks to retain more economic value, financial ownership and governance capacity within African markets.
RELATED ARTICLE: Climate Fund Managers Closes $1B Climate Adaptation Fund for Emerging Markets
James Mansfield, Managing Director of Finance Earth, said:
“Africa holds a quarter of the planet’s biodiversity, yet nature-based projects across the continent face major challenges in accessing the patient, fairly structured capital they need to succeed. Africa Nature is designed to change this by financing projects equitably and building local investment and governance structures, so that African nature assets are financed by African financial institutions. This announcement marks a critical milestone in the delivery of this vision and the culmination of our partnership with FSD Africa to date.”
Catalytic Capital to Attract Institutional Investors
FSDAi’s proposed $6.6 million cornerstone investment is intended to reduce financing barriers and attract additional institutional and domestic capital.
Early-stage nature projects often face extended development periods, uncertain revenue streams and limited access to conventional financing.
Africa Nature’s structure seeks to address these constraints while establishing commercially sustainable investment opportunities.
Ann-Marie Chidzero, Chief Investment Officer at FSD Africa Investments, said:
“Catalytic capital works hardest when it unlocks markets that would otherwise remain out of reach. By anchoring the Africa Nature Impact Fund with much needed catalytic capital, we aim to de-risk high-integrity nature projects and crowd in the institutional and local investment that African landscapes and communities urgently need This is exactly the kind of pioneering, high-impact structure FSD Africa Investments exists to support.”
Implications for Carbon Markets and Investors
For institutional investors, Africa Nature offers a potential route into African natural capital markets through a financing structure designed to address early-stage development risks.
Its emphasis on community benefit-sharing and local governance also responds to growing scrutiny of carbon market integrity.
However, achieving the fund’s ambitions will depend on successful capital mobilisation, credible carbon accounting and commercially sustainable project revenues.
The planned 2027 first close will provide an initial test of investor appetite.
More broadly, Africa Nature’s development reflects efforts to connect biodiversity finance, carbon markets and African financial institutions.
If successful, the platform could demonstrate how conservation investment can deliver measurable climate outcomes while retaining greater economic value within the communities and countries protecting Africa’s natural resources.

articles.title: Unlocking green capital flows through credit and carbon markets. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Unlocking green capital flows through credit and carbon markets.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Along with the expansion of green credit, the carbon market is expected to create additional financial resources, reducing the capital pressure on businesses undergoing green transformation.
Outstanding green credit reached over 856,000 billion VND.
Green credit is expanding, contributing to the flow of capital into sectors supporting green transformation. However, the need for large and long-term investments necessitates the development of additional capital mobilization channels, including the carbon market.
Speaking at the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" organized by the Finance and Investment Newspaper on October 14th, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh stated that, in the process of achieving the goal of net zero emissions by 2050, the demand for capital for technological innovation, transformation of production methods, efficient energy use, and reduction of greenhouse gas emissions is increasing. While other green capital mobilization channels are developing, green credit continues to play a crucial role in the transition to a low-carbon growth model.
According to the Deputy Governor, the banking sector has proactively implemented many solutions to promote green credit, directing capital flows into industries and sectors that bring environmental benefits and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Along with this, the State Bank of Vietnam is gradually perfecting the policy framework, issuing guidelines and instructions on green credit and environmental and social risk management; and encouraging credit institutions to develop strategies, internal processes, and credit products that align with green growth goals.
The implementation results show that the scale of green credit has expanded. By the end of June 2026, outstanding green credit reached over VND 856,000 billion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025. During the period 2017-2025, the average growth rate was over 20% per year. Outstanding loans are mainly concentrated in agriculture , forestry, fisheries, and biodiversity conservation, accounting for over 31%; the green energy sector accounts for nearly 28%.
In addition, loans assessed for environmental and social risks reached over 6.2 million billion VND, accounting for more than 31.33% of the total outstanding loans in the entire economy . According to Mr. Nguyen Ngoc Canh, these results demonstrate the banking system's commitment to supporting the green transformation of businesses and the economy.
In fact, at the Agricultural and Rural Development Bank ( Agribank ), green credit is being implemented in conjunction with production sectors and customer groups with a need for transformation. By the end of March 2026, the bank's outstanding green credit balance reached nearly VND 30,000 billion. In 2026, Agribank will continue to implement a VND 3,000 billion green credit program for individual customers and a VND 50,000 billion program to finance clean, high-tech agriculture.
You may also like
One notable program is the lending program linking production, processing, and consumption under the Sustainable Development Project for 1 million hectares of high-quality, low-emission rice in the Mekong Delta, with a minimum scale of 30,000 billion VND. Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank, believes that agriculture, farmers, and rural areas are both significantly impacted by climate change and have room for emission reduction in sectors such as rice cultivation, livestock farming, forestry, biomass energy, and waste treatment. Therefore, the issue is not only about providing capital for production activities, but also about financing the process of creating measurable and verifiable emission reduction results.
Credit is a crucial channel for capital flow; however, Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, believes that bank credit alone cannot meet the entire capital needs for green transformation. It is estimated that Vietnam needs approximately US$368 billion in additional investment for climate change adaptation, resilience enhancement, and emission reduction by 2040, equivalent to 6.8% of GDP annually. Of this, the need for adaptation and resilience enhancement is approximately US$254 billion, while emission reduction requires about US$114 billion. The electricity sector alone needs approximately US$136 billion in investment for power generation and transmission development between 2026 and 2030.
Mr. Bui Minh Giap affirmed: "Banks are an important channel for capital flow, but they cannot alone meet the long-term capital needs for green financing and conversion financing." Therefore, it is necessary to combine credit with green bonds, conversion bonds, equity capital, mixed financing, guarantees, and risk-sharing mechanisms. Each type of risk needs to be allocated to parties with appropriate management capabilities.
The carbon market needs to create real economic value.
Along with green credit, the carbon market is expected to unlock more resources for businesses by converting emission reduction results into economic value. According to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, by establishing quotas, measuring emission reduction results, and forming transaction prices for quotas and carbon credits, the market creates incentives for businesses to proactively invest in green transformation.
The Deputy Governor argued that when the carbon market operates effectively, the results of emission reductions can become a source of financing for businesses themselves. This would give businesses the ability to generate additional resources from their emission reductions, helping to reduce pressure on equity capital, the budget, and bank credit. In the long term, this mechanism helps diversify financing sources for green transition and facilitates more efficient credit allocation.
According to Mr. Pham Van Hoanh, Editor-in-Chief of the Finance - Investment Newspaper, the legal framework for the carbon market was established by the 2020 Environmental Protection Law and further concretized by related regulations. Decree No. 29/2026/ND-CP regulates the domestic carbon exchange; Decree No. 112/2026/ND-CP regulates the international exchange of greenhouse gas emission reduction results and carbon credits.
You may also like
Accordingly, the emission quota trading system will be implemented from June 29, 2026. The pilot phase will last until the end of 2028, before transitioning to full mandatory operation from 2029. The quota allocated to facilities in the three major emission sectors – thermal power, iron and steel, and cement – during the 2025-2026 period will reach over 511 million tons of CO₂ equivalent. During the pilot phase, the Vietnam Investment and Development Bank ( BIDV ) will be the sole clearing bank in the market.
However, the formation of new trading infrastructure is only the beginning. “If the carbon exchange is the market infrastructure, then credit policy, the banking system, and the capital market are the driving forces for the green transition,” Mr. Pham Van Hoanh emphasized.
From a banking perspective, Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha argues that the central question is not just whether banks participate in buying and selling carbon credits, but how they can finance the process of generating emission reductions and when the carbon value is sufficiently certain to be considered in credit decisions. For projects expected to generate revenue from carbon credits, the revenue generation process often lags behind the initial investment needs. Businesses need capital to prepare the project, implement technology, organize production, and measure emission reduction results; only then do they move on to verification, issuance of credits, transactions, and payments. This time gap necessitates careful assessment of cash flow and repayment capacity.
Mr. Pham Van Hoanh, Editor-in-Chief of the Finance - Investment Newspaper: A market that wants to develop sustainably needs not only an exchange, commodities, and trading regulations, but also liquidity, data, verification mechanisms, trust between buyers and sellers, and a sufficiently strong financial ecosystem to support participating entities. The implementation of emission quota trading needs to be accompanied by the ability to identify, value, and manage green capital flows, helping green transformation projects access appropriate funding.

articles.title: Green Bonds Move Deeper Into Mainstream Finance As Investor Demand Reaches Record Highs - Asianet Newsable
articles.summary: Green Bonds Move Deeper Into Mainstream Finance As Investor Demand Reaches Record Highs  Asianet Newsable
articles.full_text:
Sustainable debt is rapidly becoming one of the most influential segments of global finance as governments, companies and public institutions seek funding for climate-related investments and long-term economic resilience.
According to the latest figures from the Climate Bonds Initiative (CBI), annual issuance of GSS+ bonds, covering green, social and sustainability-linked debt instruments, has surpassed the $1 trillion mark for the third consecutive year. The growth reflects rising investor demand for projects tied to climate action and infrastructure designed to withstand future environmental and economic risks.
Recent debt offerings demonstrate the strength of market appetite. Spain's latest 20-year green bond attracted demand worth more than 20 times its €4 billion issuance target, while Italy's newly issued 12-year green bond was more than 13 times oversubscribed.
For Sean Kidney, co-founder and chief executive of the Climate Bonds Initiative, the growth represents a dramatic transformation. When the organisation began promoting green bonds in 2009, only about $2 billion worth of such debt existed globally. Today, the amount outstanding exceeds $7 trillion.
Kidney argues that investors increasingly view sustainable debt as a way to protect long-term returns in an era marked by climate threats, economic instability and rising uncertainty. Institutional investors are no longer debating whether climate risks exist. Instead, the focus has shifted toward finding enough high-quality sustainable assets to invest in.
Demand is being driven by both investors and issuers. Non-financial companies and financial institutions each account for 23 per cent of issuance, followed by development banks at 20 per cent, government-backed entities at 19 per cent and sovereign issuers at 12 per cent.
The appeal extends beyond environmental objectives. For many issuers, green bonds provide a mechanism to finance infrastructure that strengthens economic resilience while addressing climate-related challenges.
One example cited by Kidney is the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, which recently issued a €300 million green bond. The proceeds are helping finance infrastructure intended to protect the city's 14 million residents from storm surges and other climate-related threats while supporting broader economic stability.
Market expansion has also been supported by regulatory developments designed to improve transparency and credibility. Recent examples include the European Union's Green Bond Standard introduced in 2024 and China's updated green taxonomy that came into effect in late 2025.
The International Capital Market Association has also played a key role through its Green Bond Principles, which provide widely used guidelines on how bond proceeds are allocated and managed.
Meanwhile, the Climate Bonds Initiative has developed its own Climate Bonds Standard. Under the voluntary framework, 95 per cent of bond proceeds must align with strict climate objectives, while the remaining portion can be directed toward other sustainability goals.
To support consistency, financial markets have increasingly embraced taxonomies, effectively rulebooks outlining which activities qualify as green investments. The European Union's framework remains among the most comprehensive, but more than 50 jurisdictions, including China, India, South Africa, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and ASEAN, have implemented similar systems.
Differences remain between regions. The EU taxonomy allows certain new gas projects subject to strict emissions limits, while China's framework excludes fossil fuel-related projects entirely. Kidney maintains that these variations reflect different economic conditions rather than a rejection of climate science.
The sector has also faced scrutiny. Earlier projects marketed as environmentally beneficial did not always deliver intended outcomes, reinforcing the need for stronger oversight and verification. The Climate Bonds Initiative has publicly challenged transactions it believes conflict with internationally recognised climate pathways.
Despite occasional controversy, Kidney believes sustainable finance principles are gradually becoming embedded within broader capital markets. In his view, investors ultimately focus on resilience because resilience improves the likelihood that debt will be repaid.
He points to Jamaica's experience following a major hurricane in 2025. A $150 million catastrophe bond arranged by the World Bank helped support recovery efforts, and the country's long-term credit rating was later upgraded by Moody's. For investors, Kidney argues, that outcome demonstrates why resilience-focused financing is increasingly becoming a financial necessity rather than a niche sustainability product.

GreenCo Introduces New ESG Data Collection Solution
GreenCo ESG Advisory Limited has launched a new ESG data collection solution to improve the accuracy, consistency and traceability of corporate sustainability reporting.
The technology helps companies extract, consolidate and verify ESG information from electricity bills, invoices, fuel records and other supporting documents. It also provides visibility into the calculations behind reported figures.
The launch comes as businesses face increasing scrutiny over sustainability disclosures and the reliability of their underlying data.
Regulatory frameworks and emerging assurance requirements are placing greater emphasis on documented evidence, consistent methodologies and transparent reporting processes.
GreenCo’s solution addresses these demands by connecting source documentation with structured ESG datasets, reducing manual processing while strengthening data oversight.
Automating ESG Data Collection and Consolidation
The platform streamlines the collection and preparation of sustainability information from multiple sources.
Companies can upload electricity and water bills, procurement records, fuel documentation and invoices through an online form. The system then extracts relevant information into predefined reporting fields.
It also consolidates data from multiple documents into structured datasets suitable for annual sustainability reporting.
Additional capabilities include multilingual document processing, automated unit conversions and batch processing of approximately 10 to 20 files per round.
For example, companies can convert procurement quantities into kilograms or tonnes using agreed specifications. Monthly utility records can also be consolidated into annual consumption figures.
These functions aim to reduce repetitive administrative work while improving consistency across reporting periods.
Strengthening ESG Data Traceability and Assurance
A central feature is the platform’s ability to demonstrate how reported ESG figures are calculated.
Rather than displaying consolidated totals alone, the system can provide supporting source data, conversion factors, formulas and calculation steps.
This transparency allows internal reviewers to identify missing information, inconsistencies and potential calculation errors before figures enter formal disclosures.
“The quality of an ESG report ultimately depends on the quality of the data behind it. As companies prepare for increasingly rigorous reporting and assurance expectations, having a clear process to trace reported figures back to their underlying records is becoming increasingly important,” said Max Tsang, Director and Co-Founder of GreenCo. “We developed this solution to make data collection more systematic and transparent, rather than simply automating data entry.”

The functionality could support companies preparing for external assurance by improving the accessibility and documentation of supporting evidence.
However, GreenCo acknowledges that automated processing does not replace appropriate internal controls, professional review or independent assurance.
Customised Workflows Address Corporate Reporting Challenges
Unlike general-purpose AI applications, GreenCo configures its solution around each company’s reporting requirements and internal processes.
Its advisory team establishes relevant data fields, calculation methodologies, reporting formats and unit conversions according to organisational requirements.
Companies can therefore retain existing collection methodologies while reducing the manual effort required to prepare sustainability information.
“For many companies, one of the biggest challenges in ESG reporting is not understanding what needs to be disclosed, but obtaining reliable data from the people, systems and documents across the organisation,” said Stephanie Chan, Principal Consultant and Co-Owner of GreenCo. “Our objective is to help bridge that gap. By connecting source documents with structured data collection and transparent calculations, companies can spend less time on repetitive data preparation and more time reviewing whether the data makes sense and addressing any gaps identified.”
Implications for Corporate ESG Governance
For sustainability executives and investors, reliable ESG data increasingly influences disclosure quality, risk assessments and confidence in corporate performance.
GreenCo’s approach supports a transition from fragmented annual information gathering towards repeatable data management processes.
More consistent documentation can improve management oversight, support assurance preparation and help organisations identify reporting weaknesses earlier.
Alongside its technology offering, GreenCo has developed the GreenCo ESG Action Toolkit app, providing educational resources and sustainability updates.
As ESG reporting requirements evolve across jurisdictions, companies face growing pressure to demonstrate the reliability of their disclosures.
Solutions that connect reported figures directly to supporting evidence could help strengthen corporate reporting controls and improve confidence in sustainability information across global markets.

EY, Watershed Partner to Automate Carbon Reporting and ESG Compliance
- Strengthening regulatory readiness: EY US and Watershed have formed an alliance to help companies automate greenhouse gas emissions calculations and produce audit-ready sustainability data.
- Expanding emissions measurement: The partnership combines Watershed’s AI-powered platform with EY US advisory expertise to support Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions tracking, product carbon footprinting and sustainability reporting.
- Connecting data with decarbonization: The alliance aims to help organizations translate emissions data into operational decisions, improve reporting efficiency and advance corporate climate strategies.
EY US and sustainability technology company Watershed have announced a strategic alliance to help businesses strengthen carbon accounting, automate sustainability reporting and meet evolving regulatory requirements.
The partnership combines Watershed’s artificial intelligence platform with EY US sustainability advisory, implementation and program management services. Together, the companies aim to improve how organizations collect, measure and report environmental data.
The alliance addresses a growing challenge for multinational businesses. Companies must manage increasingly complex emissions inventories while responding to regulatory obligations, investor scrutiny and customer expectations.
By integrating automated data management with sustainability expertise, EY US and Watershed intend to help businesses establish more reliable reporting processes and connect environmental performance with operational decision-making.
Automating Carbon Accounting and Regulatory Reporting
Corporate emissions measurement remains technically demanding, particularly for businesses operating across multiple jurisdictions and supply chains.
Scope 1 emissions cover direct operational activities, while Scope 2 accounts for purchased energy. Scope 3 extends across upstream and downstream value chains, where data availability and consistency can present significant challenges.
The EY-Watershed Alliance will support organizations across these categories through automated greenhouse gas calculations, audit-grade data collection and standardized reporting processes.
Its capabilities also include product carbon footprinting, sustainability data management and decarbonization planning.
These services aim to reduce manual reporting requirements while improving the consistency and traceability of emissions information.
For companies facing sustainability disclosure obligations, stronger data infrastructure can help support internal controls, regulatory readiness and external assurance processes.
Derek Przybylo, EY-Watershed Alliance Leader at EY US, said: “The alliance between EY US and Watershed helps organizations move from their sustainability goals to measurable action. By combining EY US sustainability advisory, implementation and program management capabilities with Watershed’s sustainability AI platform, the EY-Watershed Alliance helps clients strengthen emissions measurement, automate reporting and build scalable sustainability solutions that support their decarbonization initiatives and regulatory readiness.”
Connecting AI-Powered Sustainability Data With Business Strategy
Beyond regulatory compliance, the partnership seeks to expand how organizations use sustainability information to guide business decisions.
Watershed’s platform provides the technology foundation for emissions measurement and reporting. EY US contributes advisory expertise to help companies integrate those capabilities into existing operations and sustainability programs.
This combination could prove particularly relevant for organizations managing complex supply chains, multiple reporting frameworks and evolving decarbonization commitments.
Automated emissions calculations can reduce administrative burdens and allow sustainability teams to focus more resources on identifying operational improvements.
Product-level carbon accounting can also support procurement decisions, supplier engagement and assessments of emissions-intensive materials.

Christian Anderson, CEO at Watershed, said: “Over the next few years, sustainability work is going to evolve. It will become more automated and action-oriented. Sustainability insights will fuel operational efficiency and resilience in addition to meeting reporting demands. Through this Alliance, the companies at the center of that shift can pair Watershed’s rigorous data foundation with EY US experience guiding organizational change.“
Implications for Corporate Governance and Investors
The alliance comes as sustainability reporting becomes increasingly connected to financial oversight, enterprise risk management and corporate governance.
For executives, the ability to produce consistent emissions data can strengthen oversight of climate commitments and improve accountability across business functions.
Investors also rely on credible sustainability disclosures to evaluate transition risks, compare corporate performance and assess exposure to carbon-intensive activities.
However, automated reporting does not eliminate the need for robust methodologies, data verification and management oversight.
Companies must still address emissions estimation uncertainties, supplier data gaps and differences between reporting requirements across jurisdictions.
The EY-Watershed Alliance seeks to address these challenges by combining technology deployment with sustainability advisory and implementation support.
For multinational organizations, the broader opportunity lies in developing reporting systems that can accommodate changing regulatory requirements without repeatedly rebuilding internal processes.
As carbon accounting becomes more integrated into corporate governance and financial decision-making, demand for scalable sustainability infrastructure is likely to grow.
The partnership reflects that shift, positioning emissions measurement not simply as a disclosure obligation but as a foundation for managing climate-related risks, operational efficiency and long-term decarbonization strategies.

articles.title: Designing carbon markets that work: How Asian policymakers are advancing credible ETS implementation - Environmental Defense Fund
articles.summary: Designing carbon markets that work: How Asian policymakers are advancing credible ETS implementation  Environmental Defense Fund
articles.full_text:
- Asia’s carbon market momentum is shifting from exploration to implementation. Governments across South and Southeast Asia are designing emissions trading systems, strengthening MRV and data infrastructure, and aligning carbon pricing with competitiveness, affordability and economic development goals.
- Capacity building and peer learning are critical to high-integrity ETS design. The ICAP Asia Summer School, delivered with EDF and partners, helped policymakers and NGOs explore global carbon market lessons and translate them into practical, regionally tailored approaches that can deliver verifiable emissions reductions at scale.
Across South and Southeast Asia, governments are moving from exploring carbon markets to designing the policies, institutions, and data systems needed to make them work. As countries work toward increasingly ambitious climate goals, emissions trading systems (ETSs) are emerging as a key tool to reduce emissions while supporting economic development and competitiveness. Many governments are now grappling with the practical challenges of implementation: building robust monitoring and reporting systems, designing markets that fit national circumstances, addressing competitiveness concerns, and ensuring carbon pricing works alongside existing climate and energy policies.
Last month, over 30 policymakers from India, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam gathered in Bangkok for a five-day intensive training on domestic emissions trading systems (ETS) to explore what it will take to build credible and effective carbon markets across the region.
The course marked the return of the International Carbon Action Partnership’s (ICAP) ETS Summer Schools funded under a new carbon pricing capacity building program from the European Commission. Alongside the Ecologic Institute and Get2C, EDF is helping to deliver this three-year global capacity building program to answer the question: How would an emissions trading system be designed and work in different countries?
Why now?
Emissions trading systems set a “cap” or limit on pollution from regulated entities, which need to surrender allowances to cover their emissions under this cap. One allowance translates to a tonne of emissions. Entities can either reduce emissions or trade allowances with each other. Over time, the cap tightens and emissions fall.
These systems are rapidly being developed in Southeast Asia as part of governments’ broader decarbonization strategies. Policymakers are looking beyond whether carbon markets can work and increasingly focusing on how to design systems that are credible, economically practical and compatible with existing policy frameworks. Questions around MRV readiness, institutional capacity, power market structures, industrial competitiveness, and interaction with other carbon pricing instruments are becoming central to ETS discussions across Asia.
A course shaped by regional concerns
The five-day course was designed off a pre-course questionnaire, which surfaced two clear priorities: building a carbon market with limited data and how those monitoring, reporting and verification systems can be strengthened over time, as well as concerns about how Asian economies can tackle climate change while still remaining competitive. Discussions focused on key decisions governments face when developing an ETS, including institutional capacities, governance frameworks, intensity-based cap, regulated prices in the power sector, market stability, and integrating carbon markets with a broader policy objective.
The sessions drew on real-world examples from guest speakers across Asia, Europe, and North America, including government regulators, capacity builders such as the World Bank and market experts from the Intercontinental Exchange, an auction and trading platform for carbon markets.
Building a carbon market in five days
Rather than presenting a single model, the program emphasized that successful carbon markets reflect local circumstances. Participants repeatedly explored how ETS design choices must account for differences in energy markets, industrial structures, institutional capacity and national development priorities.
A large share of the course was hands on, using a weeklong “Carbono” policy game where groups designed an ETS for a fictional country, presenting and defending their final design on the last day. Another interactive lesson was the half-day simulation “ETS Lab,” developed by the ICAP Secretariat and the World Bank Group that turned the tables on participants, asking them to play as regulated companies. From deciding whether to cut their emissions, trade allowances, buy credits or invest, participants were faced with the real consequences of their ETS design decisions, as well as how external factors like economic shocks could affect their compliance strategies and the ETS. Many named it as their highlight of the week.
Three key themes shared by emerging Asian ETS jurisdictions
While countries represented at the Summer School are pursuing different pathways, several lessons emerged consistently from discussions with policymakers and practitioners from around the world.
- Build credible markets from the outset: A carbon market is only credible and trustworthy if it delivers verifiable emission reductions. The foundation of this is robust data. The public and investors need confidence that a tonne emitted is a tonne accounted for. Credibility also means sending a long-term signal about the direction of the cap and ETS ambition early on. Even if the pilot phase gradually introduces elements of the ETS, this early signal helps countries plan investments.
- Carbon pricing supports competitiveness and affordability: Competitiveness and affordability concerns surfaced as the number one concern for every country in the room. Carbon markets have tested tools to address both. In particular, revenue raised from selling allowances can help companies navigate the green transition and protect households – especially low-income ones – from shouldering an undue burden. Though carbon prices are also rarely the main contributor to energy or commodity costs, which are often more influenced by fuel prices and raw materials.
- Design for your own country’s realities: While lessons from other jurisdictions are illustrative, they need to be tailored to the local circumstances, priorities and resources. In many countries in Southeast Asia for instance, the way a carbon price reaches power plants and electricity bills is not the same as Europe, where there are state-owned utilities and set prices requiring new analysis and policy adjustments. Many countries are also building an ETS alongside a carbon tax, international carbon credit trading, as well as domestic carbon crediting. These multiple systems and any overlaps need to be managed and accounted for.
Where do we go next?
Building credible carbon markets in Asia’s economies cannot be solved in a five-day course. But it does give participants a shared foundation, resources and an expert network to continue the hard work at home of building the data and legal systems these markets rely on. Many countries are no longer asking whether carbon pricing has a role to play. Instead, they are actively exploring how to build systems that deliver emissions reductions while supporting economic growth, competitiveness and energy transition objectives.
The momentum behind carbon markets in Asia is growing. The challenge now is translating that momentum into durable, high-integrity systems capable of delivering meaningful emissions reductions at scale.
EDF will continue to support high-integrity carbon markets through the ICAP Summer Schools, our regional teams and our wider carbon market programs, including how we build trust and interoperability as discussed at New York Climate Week.

articles.full_text:
ESG News Week In Review: 16 September – 30 September
Washington repealed its power plant carbon rules, Brussels handed heavy industry 121 million free permits, and Italy’s sovereign green bond still ran 13 times covered. Retreat on the rules has not yet meant retreat on the capital.
The repeal landed on 16 September. The EPA struck most of the 2024 federal greenhouse gas standards for coal and gas power plants, proposed removing what remained, and moved to rescind its 2015 greenhouse gas findings for fossil fuel generation, claiming $310 billion in savings for the power sector. What was a reported threat a fortnight earlier is now the baseline against which every US utility transition plan is written.
Europe spent the same fortnight converting climate ambition into competitiveness policy. Member states approved 121 million additional free CO2 permits for heavy industry between 2026 and 2030, worth about $9.52 billion in avoided carbon costs, then agreed to hold surplus allowances until 2030 to damp price spikes. Parliament widened CBAM to downstream steel and aluminium products while backing a temporary decarbonisation fund for 2027 to 2029. Emmanuel Macron and more than a dozen governments pressed to delay methane import rules by a year.
Capital markets did not take the hint. Italy raised roughly $9.4 billion through a 12-year sovereign green bond that drew an order book above $129 billion, covered more than 13 times, with ESG investors taking around 80% of the allocation. Hong Kong lined up as much as $2.6 billion of digital green bonds across four currencies, the World Bank Group backed $2.86 billion for Brazilian industrial decarbonisation, and the UK put $3.3 billion behind commercial fusion. Investor demand is not the scarce input; eligible assets and deliverable projects are.
The story to carry into next week is the methane import rules. The European Commission is weighing a move from January 2027 to January 2028, with non-compliance fines reaching 20% of annual turnover and intensity limits due from 2030. Industry-backed research says nearly half of EU gas imports could struggle to comply, which makes this the clearest test yet of whether energy security now outranks the bloc’s own climate timetable.
